title: Symptom control and hydration in the last days of life
blurb: Manage pain, breathlessness, nausea, agitation and secretions in the last days, and handle mouth care and hydration well.
question: Maud, 91, is dying in a care home. This evening she keeps picking at her nightdress, moaning and trying to climb out of bed. She has had two 'as required' doses of midazolam in the last 12 hours and has not passed urine since the morning. What should the nurse consider first?

teach.h: Comfort, cause and the right route
teach.body: In the last days of life the goal is comfort. NICE NG31 asks you to look for the likely cause of each symptom, treat what is reversible, use non-drug measures (repositioning, a fan, mouth care), and choose medicines with the person's preferences, other symptoms and interactions in mind. Formally: individualised, proportionate symptom management. Plainly: find out why, fix what you can, then relieve the rest gently.

teach.h: Prescribing principles in the last days (NG31 1.5)
items: Review current medicines and stop those no longer giving symptomatic benefit or that may harm, after discussion.
If oral medicines cannot be taken, use subcutaneous or intravenous routes; avoid intramuscular injections.
Start with the lowest effective dose in people new to symptom medicines and titrate.
Reassess symptoms at least daily during treatment.
Consider a syringe pump if more than 2 or 3 'as required' doses of any medicine are needed in 24 hours.
Seek specialist palliative care advice if symptoms do not improve promptly or side effects such as unwanted sedation occur.

head: Symptom
Check first
Medicines to consider
teach.caption: In obstructive bowel disorders, consider octreotide if nausea and vomiting have not improved within 24 hours of hyoscine butylbromide.

teach.body: Identify and treat reversible causes such as pulmonary oedema or pleural effusion, and consider non-drug measures like a fan and positioning. Do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness: offer it only to people known or clinically suspected to have symptomatic hypoxaemia. Medicines to consider are an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

root.label: New agitation or restlessness
root.sub: Explore causes with the person and family

teach.caption: NG31 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved symptoms or bodily needs.

preferred interval to monitor response to medicine
minimum monitoring; medicines may take this long to work

teach.caption: NG31 1.5.29–1.5.34. Watch for dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium and sedation with antimuscarinics.

teach.h: Mouth care and clinically assisted hydration
teach.body: Support the person to drink if they wish and can, checking for swallowing problems. Offer frequent mouth and lip care, help with teeth or dentures, and frequent sips; families can help if they want to. Assess hydration, preferably daily. Explain honestly: clinically assisted hydration may relieve symptoms such as thirst or delirium but can cause problems, and it is uncertain whether giving it prolongs life or whether withholding it hastens death.

steps.sub: stop if overload or not wanted

teach.h: Scenario: Maud in the care home
teach.body: Nurse Femi finds Maud, 91, restless and moaning. She has had two doses of midazolam and has not passed urine for over 12 hours. Before a third dose, Femi checks her abdomen: a full, tender bladder. With the GP's agreement a catheter is passed, and Maud settles. Femi also notes she has needed several 'as required' doses, so asks the GP to review whether a syringe pump is needed if symptoms return, and updates the anticipatory medicines plan.

teach.text: Don't reach for sedation first. A restless dying person may be in pain, have a full bladder or rectum, or be thirsty. And don't confuse the hydration monitoring minimum (at least every 12 hours) with the overall review of the dying person (at least every 24 hours).

items: Treat reversible causes first; use non-drug measures; review and stop unhelpful medicines.
Avoid IM injections; use SC or IV. Syringe pump if more than 2–3 PRN doses in 24 hours.
Lowest effective dose, reassess at least daily, seek specialist advice if not settling.
No routine oxygen for breathlessness; only for symptomatic hypoxaemia.
Secretions: reassure; monitor 4-hourly ideally, at least 12-hourly.
Frequent mouth care; assess hydration daily; CAH monitored at least every 12 hours.
Anticipatory medicines prescribed early for pain, agitation, anxiety, breathlessness, nausea and secretions.

summary: You can now assess common symptoms in the last days of life, look for reversible causes and apply NICE NG31 principles on routes, syringe pumps and anticipatory medicines. You can also give good mouth care and discuss and monitor clinically assisted hydration.

A.q: Errol, 67, has oesophageal cancer and is dying at home. He can no longer swallow. Since yesterday afternoon the district nurses have given him four separate subcutaneous 'as required' doses of morphine for pain. What should the community nurse discuss with the prescriber?
options: Switching the morphine to regular intramuscular injections
Restarting oral tablets crushed into yoghurt
Giving the same doses but at fixed six-hourly times
Starting a syringe pump for continuous symptom control
A.why: NICE NG31 rec 1.5.6: consider a syringe pump if more than 2 or 3 doses of any 'as required' medicine have been given within 24 hours.

whyNot.0: NG31 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life.
whyNot.1: He can no longer swallow, so the oral route is not appropriate.
whyNot.2: Regular bolus injections are less smooth than continuous delivery and do not follow the NG31 trigger for a syringe pump.

A.q: Dilys, 78, has metastatic lung cancer and is in her last days on a hospice ward. She feels short of breath while lying still. Her SpO2 is 96% breathing room air. Which approach does NICE NG31 support?
options: Start oxygen at 2 L/min for comfort
Use a fan and consider an opioid
Arrange urgent chest physiotherapy
Start oxygen if she becomes anxious
A.why: NG31 1.5.16–1.5.17: consider non-drug measures and an opioid, benzodiazepine or both; do not routinely start oxygen, offering it only for symptomatic hypoxaemia. Her saturation is normal.

whyNot.0: Oxygen is not started routinely for breathlessness; she is not hypoxaemic.
whyNot.2: Physiotherapy is not an NG31 breathlessness measure in the last days and may add burden.
whyNot.3: Anxiety is not hypoxaemia; oxygen is for symptomatic hypoxaemia, and anxiety may need other treatment.

A.q: Mr Chaudhry, 81, is unconscious in his last hours. Each breath now makes a gurgling sound. His son, sitting with him, asks anxiously whether his father is drowning. What is the best initial response?
options: Begin oral suctioning every hour to keep his airway clear
Sit him fully upright and start oxygen via nasal cannulae
Explain the noise is unlikely to cause him discomfort
Tell him the sound means his father needs morphine for pain
A.why: NG31 1.5.29: reassure that although the noise can be distressing, it is unlikely to cause the person discomfort, and talk about fears or concerns. Repositioning or a medicine may then be considered.

whyNot.0: Frequent suctioning can be distressing and is not the first-line response to noisy secretions.
whyNot.1: Oxygen is not indicated without suspected hypoxaemia, and full upright positioning may not be comfortable.
whyNot.3: This is inaccurate and would add to the son's distress; NG31 1.5.29 says the noise is unlikely to cause discomfort.

B.q: Desmond, 73, has heart failure and a malignant bowel obstruction from colorectal cancer. He is in his last days and keeps vomiting. Which medicine does NICE NG31 suggest considering first line?
options: Cyclizine hydrochloride
Hyoscine butylbromide
Subcutaneous metoclopramide
Subcutaneous octreotide
B.why: NG31 1.5.22: for obstructive bowel disorders consider hyoscine butylbromide first line, then octreotide if not improved within 24 hours. NG31 also notes cyclizine may worsen heart failure.

whyNot.0: NG31 gives cyclizine as an example of a medicine that may exacerbate heart failure, which Desmond has.
whyNot.2: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and is not the NG31 first-line choice in bowel obstruction.
whyNot.3: Octreotide is the second step if symptoms do not improve within 24 hours of hyoscine butylbromide.

B.q: Ama, 84, is in her last days. Yesterday the team began subcutaneous fluids as a trial because she was thirsty and newly muddled. How often, at least, should the nurse monitor for benefit or harm?
options: Every 4 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 24 hours
Every 48 hours
B.why: NG31 1.4.9: monitor at least every 12 hours for changes in symptoms or signs of dehydration and for evidence of benefit or harm.

whyNot.0: Four-hourly is the preferred interval for monitoring medicines for noisy secretions.
whyNot.2: Every 24 hours is the minimum for reviewing the dying person overall, not for assisted hydration.
whyNot.3: Two days is too long to spot fluid overload or lack of benefit.

B.q: Winston, 90, is dying on a medical ward and manages only small sips. His wife asks, 'Would a drip buy him more time?' Which reply reflects NICE NG31?
options: Yes, a drip will extend his life by several days
No, a drip will shorten his life by overloading him
It is uncertain whether a drip will prolong his life
A drip is used routinely, so the question does not arise
B.why: NG31 1.4.5: it is uncertain if clinically assisted hydration will prolong life or extend the dying process, and uncertain if not giving it will hasten death. It may relieve some symptoms but can cause problems.

whyNot.0: There is no evidence that it reliably extends life in the last days.
whyNot.1: It can cause problems such as fluid overload, but shortening life is not established.
whyNot.3: Clinically assisted hydration is an individual decision, not routine.

C.q: Irene, 66, has liver metastases and develops new abdominal pain in her last days. She has never taken an opioid. The team plan subcutaneous morphine. What principle should guide the starting dose?
options: Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate
Give a high dose to gain control quickly
Use the dose from her last hospital admission
Match the dose given to other patients on the ward
C.why: NG31 1.5.7: for people not previously given symptom control medicines, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing at least daily.

whyNot.1: A high starting dose in an opioid-naive person risks sedation and respiratory depression.
whyNot.2: She has not had opioids before, so there is no previous dose to use.
whyNot.3: Doses are individualised to the person and their response, not to other patients.

C.q: Bernard, 82, has dementia and is dying. He cannot describe pain but grimaces when turned. How should the nurse assess his pain?
options: Ask him to rate his pain on a 0–10 scale
Rely on his daughter's report of his comfort
Wait for him to call out before giving analgesia
Use a validated behavioural pain tool
C.why: NG31 1.5.14: for a person unable to explain that they are in pain, such as someone with dementia or learning disabilities, use a validated behavioural pain assessment to inform pain management.

whyNot.0: A numerical scale needs the person to understand and respond, which Bernard cannot do.
whyNot.1: Family insight helps, but a validated behavioural tool is what NG31 recommends.
whyNot.2: Waiting for vocal signs misses other behavioural signs such as grimacing and guarding.

C.q: Patricia, 68, is likely to die at home in the coming week. Her GP is planning anticipatory medicines. Which factor does NICE NG31 specifically say to take into account?
options: Whether the community nurse prefers tablets or injections
The cost of each medicine compared with oral alternatives
Her place of care and time to obtain medicines
Whether her family have given written consent
C.why: NG31 1.6.4: take into account the likelihood of symptoms, benefits and harms, the risk of sudden deterioration, and the place of care and the time it would take to obtain medicines.

whyNot.0: Route is chosen around the person's condition and ability to swallow, not a nurse's preference.
whyNot.1: Cost is not one of the NG31 factors for anticipatory prescribing.
whyNot.3: Patricia's own involvement matters; family written consent is not a requirement.

reteach.title: Why, fix, soothe
reteach.question: Faced with any distressing symptom in a dying person, what three questions should you ask in order?

blocks.body: WHY is this happening? Look for a cause: a full bladder, constipation, a drug side effect, fluid on the lungs. FIX what is reversible and sensible to fix at this stage. SOOTHE the rest: non-drug comfort first (position, fan, mouth care, presence), then medicines at the lowest effective dose by the subcutaneous route if swallowing has failed.

blocks.text: Oxygen is a treatment for hypoxaemia, not for the feeling of breathlessness. NICE NG31 says do not start it routinely in the last days of life.

explain.body: Avoid IM injections; use SC or IV when oral medicines cannot be taken. Consider a syringe pump if more than 2 or 3 'as required' doses of any medicine are given in 24 hours.

test.q: According to NICE NG31, which route should be avoided for medicines in the last days of life?
options: Subcutaneous
Intravenous
Intramuscular
Transdermal patch
test.why: NG31 1.5.5: avoid intramuscular injections; give subcutaneous or intravenous injections.

whyNot.0: Subcutaneous is the commonly used route in the last days.
whyNot.1: Intravenous is acceptable where access already exists.
whyNot.3: Transdermal and other non-injected routes can be considered according to the person's condition and preference.

explain.body: Look for unrelieved pain, a full bladder or rectum, and reversible metabolic causes. Use non-drug measures. Consider a benzodiazepine for anxiety or agitation, or an antipsychotic for delirium or agitation; seek specialist advice if uncertain or not responding.

test.q: A dying man becomes agitated. His last recorded bowel movement was six days ago. What should the nurse consider before giving sedation?
options: Starting oxygen therapy for restlessness
Withholding all fluids
Increasing his opioid dose
A full rectum causing discomfort
test.why: NG31 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved symptoms or bodily needs, for example a full bladder or rectum.

whyNot.0: Oxygen is not a treatment for agitation without hypoxaemia.
whyNot.1: Withholding fluids does not address the likely cause.
whyNot.2: Increasing opioids may worsen constipation and does not address the likely cause.

explain.body: Reassure that the noise is unlikely to cause discomfort. Consider repositioning. If distressing, consider atropine, glycopyrronium, hyoscine butylbromide or hyoscine hydrobromide. Monitor preferably every 4 hours, at least every 12 hours; medicines may take up to 12 hours to work.

test.q: Glycopyrronium was started for noisy secretions 6 hours ago and the noise continues. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue and monitor, as it may take up to 12 hours
Stop it now and switch to a different antimuscarinic
Begin hourly deep suctioning to clear the airway
Double the dose straight away to speed up its effect
test.why: NG31 1.5.33: medicines may take up to 12 hours to become effective; consider changing or stopping if secretions still cause distress after 12 hours.

whyNot.1: Switching at 6 hours is too early to judge effect.
whyNot.2: Frequent deep suctioning is distressing and not recommended as routine.
whyNot.3: Dose changes are a prescriber decision and it is too early to judge the effect.

explain.body: Help the person drink if they wish and can safely. Frequent mouth and lip care and sips. Assess hydration, preferably daily. A trial of clinically assisted hydration may help thirst or delirium; monitor at least every 12 hours; reduce or stop if harm such as fluid overload, or if no longer wanted.

test.q: During a trial of subcutaneous fluids, a dying woman develops new crackles and ankle swelling. What does NICE NG31 recommend?
options: Increase the rate to improve her thirst
Reduce or stop the fluids as there are signs of harm
Continue unchanged until the planned trial period ends
Switch to intravenous fluids at the same volume
test.why: NG31 1.4.9: reduce or stop clinically assisted hydration if there are signs of possible harm, such as fluid overload, or if the person no longer wants it.

whyNot.0: Increasing fluids would worsen the overload.
whyNot.2: Continuing despite signs of harm goes against NG31.
whyNot.3: Changing route at the same volume does not address the overload.
